this was initially Germanic and pagan. <color=#3366CC>Arian Christian</color> missionaries had been spreading Arian Christianity throughout
northern Europe, though by 700 the religion of northern Europeans was largely a mix of <color=#3366CC>Germanic paganism</color>,
Christianized paganism, and Arian Christianity. Chalcedonian Christianity had barely started to spread in northern
Europe by this time. Through the practice of simony, local princes typically auctioned off ecclesiastical offices, causing
priests and bishops to function as though they were yet another noble under the patronage of the prince. In contrast, a
network of <color=#3366CC>monasteries</color> had sprung up as monks sought separation from the world. These monasteries remained
independent from local princes, and as such constituted the "church" for most northern Europeans during this time.
Being independent from local princes, they increasingly stood out as centres of learning, of scholarship, and as
religious centres where individuals could receive spiritual or monetary assistance.
The interaction between the culture of the newcomers, their warband loyalties, the remnants of classical culture, and
Christian influences, produced a new model for society, based in part on <color=#3366CC>feudal obligations</color>. The centralized
administrative systems of the Romans did not withstand the changes, and the institutional support for <color=#3366CC>chattel slavery</color>
largely disappeared. The Visigoths and Lombards abandoned Arianism for Nicene Christianity and the formerly pagan
Anglo-Saxons, Thuringians, and <color=#3366CC>Bavarians</color> converted to Christianity between the late 6th and mid-8th centuries but the
<color=#3366CC>Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom in Iberia</color> (711–720s) — the most organized and legally sophisticated
Germanic Latin Christian kingdom of the era — left the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of the Franks</color> ("Francia"), Kingdom of the Lombards
(on the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color>) and <color=#3366CC>petty Anglo-Saxon kingdoms</color> (in the <color=#3366CC>British Isles</color>) as the only significant Latin Christian
realms. Within these three realms, however, the cultural influence of the Latin Church — including its <color=#3366CC>prohibitions on</color>
<color=#3366CC>cousin marriage</color>, polygamy, and remarriage within kin groups — ran longest and cut deepest, gradually eroding the
extended <color=#3366CC>clans</color> and <color=#3366CC>kinship</color> groups that had long organized Western European society.
Italy
The Lombards, who first entered Italy in 568 under <color=#3366CC>Alboin</color>, carved out a state in the north, with its capital at Pavia. At
first, they were unable to conquer the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Ducatus Romanus, and <color=#3366CC>Calabria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Apulia</color>. The next
two hundred years were occupied in trying to conquer these territories from the Byzantine Empire.
The Lombard state was relatively Romanized, at least when compared to the Germanic kingdoms in northern Europe. It
was highly decentralized at first, with the territorial dukes having practical sovereignty in their duchies, especially in the
southern duchies of <color=#3366CC>Spoleto</color> and Benevento. For a decade following the death of Cleph in 575, the Lombards did not
even elect a king; this period is called the Rule of the Dukes. The first written legal code was composed in poor Latin in
643: the Edictum Rothari. It was primarily the codification of the oral legal tradition of the people.
The Lombard state was well-organized and stabilized by the end of the long reign of <color=#3366CC>Liutprand</color> (717–744), but its
collapse was sudden. Unsupported by the dukes, King Desiderius was defeated and forced to surrender his kingdom to
Charlemagne in 774. The Lombard kingdom ended and a period of Frankish rule was initiated. The Frankish king <color=#3366CC>Pepin</color>
<color=#3366CC>the Short</color> had, by the Donation of Pepin, given the pope the "<color=#3366CC>Papal States</color>" and the territory north of that swath of
papally-governed land was ruled primarily by Lombard and Frankish vassals of the Holy Roman Emperor until the rise
of the <color=#3366CC>city-states</color> in the 11th and 12th centuries.
From the 650s onward, the Mediterranean became a <color=#3366CC>battleground between Arab and Byzantine naval forces</color>, with both
sides launching raids and counterraids against islands and coastal settlements and engaging in a naval arms race. In
the latter part of the conflict, the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Venice</color> emerged as an important ally of the Byzantines.
In the south, a period of chaos began. The Duchy of Benevento maintained its sovereignty in the face of the
pretensions of both the Western and Eastern Empires. In the 9th century, the Muslims conquered Sicily. The cities on
the <color=#3366CC>Tyrrhenian Sea</color> departed from Byzantine allegiance. Various states owing various nominal allegiances fought
constantly over territory until events came to a head in the early 11th century with the coming of the <color=#3366CC>Normans</color>, who
conquered the whole of the south by the end of the century.
Britain
<color=#3366CC>Roman Britain</color> was in a state of political and economic collapse at the time of the Roman departure c. 400. A series of
settlements (traditionally referred to as an invasion) by <color=#3366CC>Germanic peoples</color> began in the early fifth century, and by the
sixth century the island would consist of many small kingdoms engaged in ongoing warfare with each other. The
Germanic kingdoms are now collectively referred to as <color=#3366CC>Anglo-Saxons</color>. Christianity began to take hold among the
Anglo-Saxons in the sixth century, with 597 given as the traditional date for its large-scale adoption.
Western Britain (<color=#3366CC>Wales</color>), eastern and northern Scotland (Pictland) and the <color=#3366CC>Scottish highlands</color> and isles continued their
separate evolution. The <color=#3366CC>Irish</color> descended and Irish-influenced people of western Scotland were Christian from the fifth
century onward, the Picts adopted Christianity in the sixth century under the influence of <color=#3366CC>Columba</color>, and the Welsh had
been Christian since the Roman era.
The <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Northumbria</color> was the pre-eminent power c. 600–700, absorbing several weaker Anglo-Saxon and
Brythonic kingdoms, while <color=#3366CC>Mercia</color> held a similar status c. 700–800. <color=#3366CC>Wessex</color> would absorb all of the kingdoms in the
south, both Anglo-Saxon and Briton. In Wales consolidation of power would not begin until the ninth century under the
descendants of Merfyn Frych of <color=#3366CC>Gwynedd</color>, establishing a hierarchy that would last until the Norman invasion of Wales
The first <color=#3366CC>Viking</color> raids on Britain began before 800, increasing in scope and destructiveness over time. In 865 a large,
well-organized <color=#3366CC>Danish</color> Viking army (called the Great Heathen Army) attempted a conquest, breaking or diminishing
Anglo-Saxon power everywhere but in Wessex. Under the leadership of <color=#3366CC>Alfred the Great</color> and his descendants, Wessex
would at first survive, then coexist with, and eventually conquer the Danes. It would then establish the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of</color>
<color=#3366CC>England</color> and rule until the establishment of an Anglo-Danish kingdom under <color=#3366CC>Cnut</color>, and then again until the <color=#3366CC>Norman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Invasion</color> of 1066.
Viking raids and invasion were no less dramatic for the north. Their defeat of the Picts in 839 led to a lasting <color=#3366CC>Norse</color>
heritage in northernmost Scotland, and it led to the combination of the Picts and Gaels under the House of Alpin, which
became the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Alba</color>, the predecessor of the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Scotland</color>. The Vikings combined with the Gaels of the
<color=#3366CC>Hebrides</color> to become the Gall-Gaidel and establish the Kingdom of the Isles.
Frankish Empire
The <color=#3366CC>Merovingians</color> established themselves in the power vacuum of the former Roman provinces in Gaul, and <color=#3366CC>Clovis I</color>
converted to Christianity following his victory over the Alemanni at the Battle of Tolbiac (496), laying the foundation of
the <color=#3366CC>Frankish Empire</color>, the dominant state of early medieval Western <color=#3366CC>Christendom</color>. The Frankish kingdom grew through
a complex development of conquest, patronage, and alliance building. Due to <color=#3366CC>salic custom</color>, inheritance rights were
absolute, and all land was divided equally among the sons of a dead land holder. This meant that, when the king
granted a prince land in reward for service, that prince and all of his descendants had an irrevocable right to that land
that no future king could undo. Likewise, those princes (and their sons) could sublet their land to their own vassals, who
could in turn sublet the land to lower sub-vassals. This all had the effect of weakening the power of the king as his
kingdom grew, since the result was that the land became controlled not just by more princes and vassals, but by
multiple layers of vassals. This also allowed his nobles to attempt to build their own power base, though given the strict
salic tradition of hereditary kingship, few would ever consider overthrowing the king.
This increasingly fragmented arrangement was highlighted by <color=#3366CC>Charles Martel</color>, who as Mayor of the Palace was
effectively the strongest prince in the kingdom. His accomplishments were highlighted, not just by his famous defeat of
invading Muslims at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Tours</color>, which is typically considered the battle that saved Europe from Muslim
conquest, but by the fact that he greatly expanded Frankish influence. It was under his patronage that Boniface
expanded Frankish influence into Germany by rebuilding the German church, with the result that, within a century, the
German church was the strongest church in western Europe. Yet despite this, Charles Martel refused to overthrow the
Frankish king. His son, Pepin the Short, inherited his power, and used it to further expand Frankish influence. Unlike his
father, however, Pepin decided to seize the Frankish kingship. Given how strongly Frankish culture held to its principle
of inheritance, few would support him if he attempted to overthrow the king. Instead, he sought the assistance of Pope
Zachary, who was himself newly vulnerable due to fallout with the Byzantine Emperor over the Iconoclastic
Controversy. Pepin agreed to support the pope and to give him land (the Donation of Pepin, which created the <color=#3366CC>Papal</color>
<color=#3366CC>States</color>) in exchange for being consecrated as the new Frankish king. Given that Pepin's claim to the kingship was now
based on an authority higher than Frankish custom, no resistance was offered to Pepin. With this, the Merovingian line
of kings ended, and the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian</color> line began.
Pepin's son <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> continued in the footsteps of his father and grandfather. He further expanded and
consolidated the Frankish kingdom (now commonly called the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Empire</color>). His reign also saw a cultural rebirth,
commonly called the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color>. Though the exact reasons are unclear, Charlemagne was crowned
"Roman Emperor" by <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo III</color> on Christmas Day, 800. Upon Charlemagne's death, his empire had united much of
modern-day France, western Germany and northern Italy. The years after his death illustrated how Germanic his
empire remained. Rather than an orderly succession, his empire was divided in accordance with Frankish inheritance
custom, which resulted in instability that plagued his empire until the last king of a united empire, <color=#3366CC>Charles the Fat</color>, died
in 887, which resulted in a permanent split of the empire into <color=#3366CC>West Francia</color> and <color=#3366CC>East Francia</color>. West Francia would be
ruled by Carolingians until 987 and East Francia until 911, after which time the partition of the empire into France and
Germany was complete.
Feudalism
Around 800 there was a return to systematic agriculture in the form of the open field, or strip, system. A manor would
have several fields, each subdivided into 1 acre strips of land. An acre measured one "furlong" of 220 yards by one
"chain" of 22 yards (that is, about 200 m by 20 m). A furlong (from "furrow long") was considered to be the distance an
ox could plough before taking a rest; the strip shape of the acre field also reflected the difficulty in turning early heavy
ploughs. In the idealized form of the system, each family got thirty such strips of land. The three-field system of <color=#3366CC>crop</color>
<color=#3366CC>rotation</color> was first developed in the 9th century: wheat or rye was planted in one field, the second field had a
nitrogen-fixing crop, and the third was fallow.
Compared to the earlier two-field system, a three-field system allowed for significantly more land to be put under
cultivation. Even more important, the system allowed for two harvests a year, reducing the risk that a single crop failure
will lead to famine. Three-field agriculture created a surplus of oats that could be used to feed horses. This surplus
allowed for the replacement of the ox by the horse after the introduction of the padded horse collar in the 12th century.
Because the system required a major rearrangement of real estate and of the social order, it took until the 11th century
before it came into general use. The heavy wheeled plough was introduced in the late 10th century. It required greater
animal power and promoted the use of teams of oxen. Illuminated manuscripts depict two-wheeled ploughs with both a
mouldboard, or curved metal ploughshare, and a coulter, a vertical blade in front of the ploughshare. The Romans had
used light, wheel-less ploughs with flat iron shares that often proved unequal to the heavy soils of northern Europe.
The return to systemic agriculture coincided with the introduction of a new social system called <color=#3366CC>feudalism</color>. This system
featured a hierarchy of reciprocal obligations. Each man was bound to serve his superior in return for the latter's
protection. This made for confusion of territorial sovereignty since allegiances were subject to change over time and
were sometimes mutually contradictory. Feudalism allowed the state to provide a degree of public safety despite the
continued absence of bureaucracy and written records.
Manors became largely self-sufficient, and the volume of trade along long-distance routes and in market towns declined
during this period, though never ceased entirely. Roman roads decayed and long-distance trade depended more
heavily on water transport.
Viking Age
The Viking Age spans the period roughly between the late 8th and mid-11th centuries in <color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Britain</color>,
following the Germanic Iron Age (and the Vendel Age in Sweden). During this period, the <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color>, Scandinavian
warriors and traders raided and explored most parts of <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, <color=#3366CC>south-western Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>northern Africa</color>, and north-eastern
North America.
With the means to travel (longships and open water), desire for goods led Scandinavian traders to explore and develop
extensive trading partnerships in new territories. Some of the most important trading ports during the period include
both existing and ancient cities such as <color=#3366CC>Aarhus</color>, Ribe, Hedeby, Vineta, Truso, Kaupang, Birka, <color=#3366CC>Bordeaux</color>, York, <color=#3366CC>Dublin</color>,
and Aldeigjuborg.
Viking raiding expeditions were separate from, though coexisted with, regular trading expeditions. Apart from exploring
Europe via its oceans and rivers, with the aid of their advanced navigational skills, they extended their trading routes
across vast parts of the continent. They also engaged in warfare, looting and enslaving numerous Christian
communities of medieval Europe for centuries, contributing to the development of feudal systems in Europe.
Eastern Europe
In the beginning of the period, the <color=#3366CC>Slavic tribes</color> started to expand aggressively into Central and Southeastern Europe,
including former Byzantine possessions in the Balkans. The first attested <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> polity was the so-called Samo's
Empire, followed by <color=#3366CC>Great Moravia</color>, Duchy of Bohemia, Duchy of Croatia and Serbia, also emerging under the aegis of
the Frankish Empire in the early 9th century. Great Moravia was ultimately overrun by the Magyars, who invaded the
Pannonian Basin around 896.
After the <color=#3366CC>Christianization of the First Bulgarian Empire</color> (c. 864) and with <color=#3366CC>key support from Byzantine scholars</color>, the early
Cyrillic alphabet, purpose-built for Slavic phonology, was developed there. An increasing rivalry between the Greek
East and Latin West was then expressed in an intense <color=#3366CC>missionary competition</color> through the 9th and 10th centuries, in
which <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic</color> played an important role. While Moravia (c. 863), Bohemia (c. 884) Croatia (by 900), and <color=#3366CC>Poland (966)</color>
were drawn into the Latin West, the Serbs (c. 870) and <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus' (988)</color> embraced Cyrillic and instead linked
themselves with the Greek East. In those areas, the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> influenced almost every aspect of cultural and
political development, including the preeminence of Caesaropapism and the spread of <color=#3366CC>Eastern Christianity</color>.
Turkic and Iranian invaders from <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> pressured the agricultural populations both in the Byzantine <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color> and
in Central Europe creating a number of successor states in the Pontic steppes. After the dissolution of the <color=#3366CC>Hunnic</color>

<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Western Turkic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Avar Khaganates</color> dominated territories from Pannonia to the <color=#3366CC>Caspian Sea</color> before being
replaced by the short lived Old Great Bulgaria and the more successful <color=#3366CC>Khazar Khaganate</color> north of the Black Sea and
the Magyars in Central Europe.
The <color=#3366CC>Khazars</color> were a nomadic Turkic people who managed to develop a multiethnic commercial state which owed its
success to the control of much of the waterway trade between Europe and Central Asia. The Khazars also exacted
tribute from the <color=#3366CC>Alani</color>, Magyars, various <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> tribes, the Crimean Goths, and the Greeks of <color=#3366CC>Crimea</color>. Through a
network of Jewish itinerant merchants, or Radhanites, they were in contact with the trade emporia of India and Spain.
Once they found themselves confronted by <color=#3366CC>Arab expansionism</color>, the Khazars pragmatically allied themselves with
Constantinople and clashed with the <color=#3366CC>Caliphate</color>. Despite initial setbacks, they managed to recover <color=#3366CC>Derbent</color> and
eventually penetrated as far south as Caucasian Iberia, <color=#3366CC>Caucasian Albania</color> and <color=#3366CC>Armenia</color>. In doing so, they effectively
blocked the northward expansion of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> into <color=#3366CC>Eastern Europe</color> even before khan Tervel achieved the same at the
<color=#3366CC>Second Arab Siege of Constantinople</color> and several decades before the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Tours</color> in Western Europe. Islam
eventually penetrated into Eastern Europe in the 920s when <color=#3366CC>Volga Bulgaria</color> exploited the decline of Khazar power in
the region to adopt Islam from the <color=#3366CC>Baghdad</color> missionaries. The state religion of Khazaria, <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, disappeared as a
political force with the fall of Khazaria, while Islam of Volga Bulgaria has survived in the region up to the present.
Bulgaria
In 632 the <color=#3366CC>Bulgars</color> established the khanate of Old Great Bulgaria under the leadership of Kubrat. The Khazars
managed to oust the Bulgars from Southern Ukraine into lands along middle <color=#3366CC>Volga</color> (<color=#3366CC>Volga Bulgaria</color>) and along lower
<color=#3366CC>Danube</color> (<color=#3366CC>Danube Bulgaria</color>).
In 681 the Bulgars founded a powerful and ethnically diverse state that played a defining role in the history of early
medieval Southeastern Europe. Bulgaria withstood the pressure from Pontic steppe tribes like the <color=#3366CC>Pechenegs</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Khazars</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Cumans</color>, and in 806 destroyed the <color=#3366CC>Avar</color> Khanate. The Danube Bulgars were quickly slavicized and,
despite constant campaigning against Constantinople, accepted Christianity from the Byzantine Empire. Through the
efforts of missionaries <color=#3366CC>Cyril and Methodius</color>, mainly their disciples like Clement of Ohrid and Naum, the spread, initially
of the <color=#3366CC>Glagolitic</color>, and later of the <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic</color> alphabet, developed in the capital Preslav. The local vernacular dialect, now
known as <color=#3366CC>Old Bulgarian</color> or Old Church Slavonic, was established as the language of books and liturgy among
<color=#3366CC>Orthodox Christian</color> Slavs.
After the adoption of <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> in 864, Bulgaria became a cultural and spiritual hub of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color> Slavic
world. The <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic script</color> was developed around 885–886, and was afterwards also introduced with books to Serbia and
<color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus'</color>. Literature, art, and architecture were thriving with the establishment of the Preslav and Ohrid Literary
Schools along with the distinct Preslav Ceramics School. In 927 the Bulgarian Orthodox Church was the first European
national Church to gain independence with its own Patriarch while conducting services in the vernacular <color=#3366CC>Old Church</color>
<color=#3366CC>Slavonic</color>.
Under <color=#3366CC>Simeon I</color> (893–927), the state was the largest and one of the most powerful political entities of Europe, and it
consistently threatened the existence of the Byzantine empire. From the middle of the 10th century Bulgaria was in
decline as it entered a social and spiritual turmoil. It was in part due to Simeon's devastating wars, but was also
exacerbated by a series of successful Byzantine military campaigns. Bulgaria was conquered after a long resistance in
Kievan Rus'
Led by a Varangian dynasty, the <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus'</color> controlled the <color=#3366CC>routes connecting Northern Europe to Byzantium</color> and to the
Orient (for example: the <color=#3366CC>Volga trade route</color>). The Kievan state began with the rule (882–912) of <color=#3366CC>Prince Oleg</color>, who
extended his control from <color=#3366CC>Novgorod</color> southwards along the <color=#3366CC>Dnieper</color> river valley in order to protect trade from <color=#3366CC>Khazar</color>
incursions from the east and moved his capital to the more strategic <color=#3366CC>Kiev</color>. <color=#3366CC>Sviatoslav I</color> (died 972) achieved the first
major expansion of Kievan Rus' territorial control, fighting a war of conquest against the <color=#3366CC>Khazar Empire</color> and inflicting a
serious blow on <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>. A Rus' attack (967 or 968), instigated by the Byzantines, led to the collapse of the Bulgarian
state and the occupation of the east of the country by the Rus'. An ensuing direct military confrontation between the
Rus' and Byzantium (970–971) ended with a Byzantine victory (971). The Rus' withdrew and the Byzantine Empire
incorporated eastern Bulgaria. Both before and after their <color=#3366CC>conversion to Christianity</color> (conventionally dated 988 under
<color=#3366CC>Vladimir I of Kiev</color>—known as Vladimir the Great), the Rus' also embarked on predatory military campaigns against the
Byzantine Empire, some of which resulted in trade treaties. The importance of Russo-Byzantine relations to
Constantinople was highlighted by the fact that Vladimir I of Kiev, son of <color=#3366CC>Svyatoslav I</color>, became the only foreigner to
marry (989) a Byzantine princess of the Macedonian dynasty (which ruled the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> from 867 to
1056), a singular honour sought in vain by many other rulers.
Transmission of learning
With the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> and with urban centres in decline, <color=#3366CC>literacy</color> and learning decreased in the
West. De-urbanization reduced the scope of education, and by the 6th century teaching and learning moved to
monastic and cathedral schools, with the study of biblical texts at the centre of education. The education of the laity
continued with little interruption in Italy, Spain, and the southern part of <color=#3366CC>Gaul</color>, where Roman influences lasted longer. In
the 7th century, however, learning expanded in Ireland and the Celtic lands, where Latin was a foreign language and
Latin texts were eagerly studied and taught. The <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color> of classical education appeared in the
<color=#3366CC>Carolingian Empire</color> in the 8th century.
In the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire</color> (Byzantium), learning (in the sense of formal education involving literature) was
maintained at a higher level than in the West. The classical education system, which would persist for hundreds of

years, emphasized <color=#3366CC>grammar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Latin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greek</color>, and <color=#3366CC>rhetoric</color>. Pupils read and reread classic works and wrote essays
imitating their style. By the 4th century, this education system was Christianized. In De Doctrina Christiana (started 396,
completed 426), <color=#3366CC>Augustine</color> explained how classical education fits into the Christian worldview: Christianity is a religion
of the book, so Christians must be literate. <color=#3366CC>Tertullian</color> was more skeptical of the value of classical learning, asking "What
indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?"
Natural philosophy
In the ancient world, Greek was the primary language of <color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color>. Organized research and teaching about
the natural world was mainly carried on in the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic</color> side of the Roman empire, and in Greek. Late Roman
attempts to translate Greek writings into Latin had limited success. As the import of papyrus ceased and knowledge of
Greek declined, the Latin West found itself cut off from Greek learning. The period between the 4th and the 8th
centuries was the era of the "Latin Encyclopedists". The most popular and notable of their works was Etymologiae, a
vast compendium of human knowledge at the time, including mathematics, geometry, astronomy, medicine, animals,
the physical world, geography, metals and rocks compiled by Bishop <color=#3366CC>Isidore of Seville</color> (c. 560-636).
The study of nature was pursued more for practical reasons than as an abstract inquiry: the need to care for the sick
led to the study of medicine and of ancient texts on drugs; the need for monks to determine the proper time to pray led
them to study the motion of the stars; and the need to compute the date of Easter led them to study and teach
mathematics and the motions of the Sun and Moon.
Carolingian Renaissance
In the late 8th century, there was renewed interest in <color=#3366CC>Classical Antiquity</color> as part of the Carolingian Renaissance.
Charlemagne carried out a reform in <color=#3366CC>education</color>. The English monk <color=#3366CC>Alcuin of York</color> elaborated a project of scholarly
development aimed at resuscitating classical knowledge by establishing programs of study based upon the seven

<color=#3366CC>liberal arts</color>: the trivium, or literary education (<color=#3366CC>grammar</color>, <color=#3366CC>rhetoric</color>, and <color=#3366CC>dialectic</color>), and the quadrivium, or scientific

education (<color=#3366CC>arithmetic</color>, <color=#3366CC>geometry</color>, <color=#3366CC>astronomy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>music</color>). From 787 on, <color=#3366CC>decrees</color> began to circulate recommending the
restoration of old schools and the founding of new ones across the empire.
Institutionally, these new schools were either under the responsibility of a <color=#3366CC>monastery</color> (monastic schools), a <color=#3366CC>cathedral</color>, or
a noble court. The teaching of <color=#3366CC>dialectic</color> (a discipline that corresponds to today's <color=#3366CC>logic</color>) was responsible for the increase
in the interest in speculative inquiry; from this interest would follow the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Scholastic</color> tradition of <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>
<color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>. In the 12th and 13th centuries, many of those schools founded under the auspices of Charlemagne,
especially cathedral schools, would become universities.
Byzantium's golden age
Byzantium's great intellectual achievement was the <color=#3366CC>Corpus Juris Civilis</color> ("Body of Civil Law"), a massive compilation of
<color=#3366CC>Roman law</color> made under <color=#3366CC>Justinian</color> (r. 528–565). The work includes a section called the Digesta which abstracts the
principles of Roman law in such a way that they can be applied to any situation. The level of literacy was considerably
higher in the Byzantine Empire than in the Latin West. Elementary education was much more widely available,
sometimes even in the countryside. Secondary schools still taught the <color=#3366CC>Iliad</color> and other classics.
As for higher education, the <color=#3366CC>Neoplatonic Academy</color> in <color=#3366CC>Athens</color> was closed in 526. There was also a school in Alexandria
which remained open until the Arab conquest (640). The University of Constantinople, founded by Emperor Theodosius
II (425), seems to have dissolved around this time. It was refounded by Emperor Michael III in 849. Higher education in
this period focused on rhetoric, although <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>'s logic was covered in simple outline. Under the Macedonian dynasty
(867–1056), Byzantium enjoyed a golden age and a revival of classical learning. There was little original research, but
many lexicons, anthologies, encyclopedias, and commentaries.
Islamic learning
In the course of the 11th century, Islam's scientific knowledge began to reach Western Europe, via Islamic Spain. The
works of <color=#3366CC>Euclid</color> and <color=#3366CC>Archimedes</color>, lost in the West, were translated from Arabic to Latin in Spain. The modern
<color=#3366CC>Hindu–Arabic numeral system</color>, including a notation for zero, was developed by Hindu mathematicians in the 5th and
6th centuries. Muslim mathematicians learned of it in the 7th century and added a notation for decimal fractions in the
9th and 10th centuries. Around 1000, Gerbert of Aurillac (later <color=#3366CC>Pope Sylvester II</color>) made an <color=#3366CC>abacus</color> with counters
engraved with <color=#3366CC>Arabic numerals</color>. A treatise by <color=#3366CC>Al-Khwārizmī</color> on how to perform calculations with these numerals was
translated into Latin in Spain in the 12th century.
Monasteries
<color=#3366CC>Monasteries</color> were targeted in the eighth and ninth centuries by <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color> who invaded the coasts of northern Europe.
They were targeted not only because they stored books but also precious objects that were looted by invaders. In the
earliest monasteries, there were no special rooms set aside as a library, but from the sixth century onwards libraries
became an essential aspect of monastic life in Western Europe. The <color=#3366CC>Benedictines</color> placed books in the care of a
librarian who supervised their use. In some monastic reading rooms, valuable books would be chained to shelves, but
there were also lending sections as well. Copying was also another important aspect of monastic libraries, this was
undertaken by resident or visiting monks and took place in the scriptorium. In the Byzantine world, religious houses
rarely maintained their own copying centres. Instead they acquired donations from wealthy donors. In the tenth century,
the largest collection in the Byzantine world was found in the monasteries of <color=#3366CC>Mount Athos</color> (modern-day Greece), which
accumulated over 10,000 books. Scholars travelled from one monastery to another in search of the texts they wished to
study. Travelling monks were often given funds to buy books, and certain monasteries which held a reputation for
intellectual activities welcomed travelling monks who came to copy manuscripts for their own libraries. One of these
was the monastery of Bobbio in Italy, which was founded by the Irish abbot Columbanus in 614, and by the ninth
century boasted a catalogue of 666 manuscripts, including religious works, classical texts, histories and mathematical
treatises.
Christianity West and East
From the early Christians, early medieval Christians inherited a church united by major creeds, a stable <color=#3366CC>Biblical canon</color>,
and a well-developed philosophical tradition. The history of medieval Christianity traces Christianity during the Middle
Ages—the period after the fall of the Western Roman Empire until the <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color>. The institutional
structure of Christianity in the west during this period is different from what it would become later in the Middle Ages. As
opposed to the later church, the church of the Early Middle Ages consisted primarily of the monasteries. The practice of
simony has caused the ecclesiastical offices to become the property of local princes, and as such the monasteries
constituted the only church institution independent of the local princes. In addition, the <color=#3366CC>papacy</color> was relatively weak, and
its power was mostly confined to central Italy. Individualized religious practice was uncommon, as it typically required
membership in a religious order, such as the <color=#3366CC>Order of Saint Benedict</color>. Religious orders would not proliferate until the
high Middle Ages. For the typical Christian at this time, religious participation was largely confined to occasionally
receiving mass from wandering monks. Few would receive this as often as once a month. By the end of this period,
individual practice of religion was becoming more common, as monasteries started to transform into something
approximating modern churches, where some monks might even give occasional sermons.
During the period of the Byzantine Papacy (537–752), the <color=#3366CC>bishops of Rome</color> required Byzantine approval of their
elevation, and many bishops were selected from among the apocrisiarii, ambassadors to the Byzantine court in
Constantinople. Before becoming the Bishop of Rome, <color=#3366CC>Pope Gregory I</color> (r. 590–604) - known later as "St. Gregory the
Great" and as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers - first served as an ambassador to Constantinople for 7
years. After his elevation, however, Gregory used his office as a temporal power, expanded Rome's missionary efforts
to the British Isles, and laid the foundations for the expansion of monastic orders. In 607, Boniface III became the first
Bishop of Rome to use the title <color=#3366CC>Pope</color>. Roman church traditions and practices gradually replaced local variants,
including <color=#3366CC>Celtic Christianity</color> in the <color=#3366CC>British Isles</color>. Various barbarian tribes went from raiding and pillaging the island to
invading and settling. In the East, the conquests of Islam reduced the power of the Greek-speaking patriarchates.
Christianization of the West
The Roman Church, the only centralized institution to survive the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> intact, was the sole
unifying cultural influence in the West, preserving Latin learning, maintaining the art of writing, and preserving a
centralized administration through its network of <color=#3366CC>bishops</color> ordained in succession. In Europe, a formalized institution of
marriage was established. The proscribed degree of <color=#3366CC>consanguinity</color> varied, but the custom made marriages annullable
by application to the Pope. The Early Middle Ages are characterized by the urban control of bishops and the territorial
control exercised by dukes and counts. The rise of <color=#3366CC>urban communes</color> marked the beginning of the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color>.
The Christianization of Germanic tribes began in the 4th century with the Goths and continued throughout the Early
Middle Ages, led in the 6th to 7th centuries by the Hiberno-Scottish mission and replaced in the 8th to 9th centuries by
the Anglo-Saxon mission, with Anglo-Saxons like <color=#3366CC>Alcuin</color> playing an important role in the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color>.
Boniface, the Apostle of the Germans, propagated Christianity in the Frankish Empire during the 8th century. He helped
shape Western Christianity, and many of the dioceses he proposed remain until today. After his martyrdom, he was
quickly hailed as a saint. By 1000, even <color=#3366CC>Iceland</color> had become Christian, leaving only more remote parts of Europe
(<color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color>, the Baltic, and Finnic lands) to be Christianized during the High Middle Ages.
Europe in 1000
While the assumption that Europeans feared the world would end in the year 1000 is popular today, such beliefs were
largely confined to a few select monasteries in France. Ordinary clerks used regnal years, e.g. the 4th year of the reign
of Robert II (the Pious) of France. The use of the modern "anno domini" system of dating was largely confined to
chroniclers of universal history, such as the <color=#3366CC>Venerable Bede</color>.
Western Europe remained less developed compared to the Islamic world, with its vast network of caravan trade, or
China, at this time the world's most populous empire under the <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color>. <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> had a population of about
300,000, but Rome had a mere 35,000 and Paris 20,000. By contrast, <color=#3366CC>Córdoba</color>, in Islamic Spain, at this time the
world's largest city contained 450,000 inhabitants. The <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color> had a trade network in northern Europe, including a
<color=#3366CC>route connecting the Baltic to Constantinople</color> through Russia, as did the Radhanites.
With nearly the entire nation freshly ravaged by the Vikings, England was in a desperate state. The long-suffering
English later responded with a massacre of Danish settlers in 1002, leading to a round of reprisals and finally to Danish
rule (1013), though England regained independence shortly after. Christianization made rapid progress and proved
itself the long-term solution to the problem of barbarian raiding. The territories of Scandinavia were soon to be fully
Christianized Kingdoms: <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color> in the 10th century, <color=#3366CC>Norway</color> in the 11th, and <color=#3366CC>Sweden</color>, the country with the least
raiding activity, in the 12th. <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus</color>, recently converted to Orthodox Christianity, flourished as the largest state in
Europe. Iceland, <color=#3366CC>Greenland</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> were all declared Christian about 1000.
North of Italy, where masonry construction was never extinguished, stone construction was replacing timber in
important structures. Deforestation of the densely wooded continent was under way. The 10th century marked a return
of urban life, with the Italian cities doubling in population. <color=#3366CC>London</color>, abandoned for many centuries, was again England's
main economic centre by 1000. By 1000, <color=#3366CC>Bruges</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ghent</color> held regular trade fairs behind castle walls, a tentative
return of economic life to western Europe.
In the culture of Europe, several features surfaced soon after 1000 that mark the end of the Early Middle Ages: the rise
of the <color=#3366CC>medieval communes</color>, the reawakening of city life, and the appearance of the <color=#3366CC>burgher class</color>, the founding of the
first universities, the rediscovery of <color=#3366CC>Roman law</color>, and the beginnings of vernacular literature.
In 1000, the papacy was firmly under the control of German Emperor <color=#3366CC>Otto III</color>, or "emperor of the world" as he styled
himself. But later church reforms enhanced its independence and prestige: the <color=#3366CC>Cluniac movement</color>, the building of the
first great Transalpine stone cathedrals and the collation of the mass of accumulated decretals into a formulated <color=#3366CC>canon</color>
<color=#3366CC>law</color>. Meanwhile, a new Central European power was taking shape, and on <color=#3366CC>Christmas Day</color> of 1000, <color=#3366CC>Stephen I</color> was
crowned as the first king of Hungary, stabilising the country, which had been ruled by grand princes. Like the Civitas
Schinesghe, which was also consolidating at the time, the country was seen as a promising political and trading
partner, and a federati (ally) by the emperor.
Middle East
Rise of Islam
Consult particular article for details
The rise of Islam begins around the time <color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color> and his followers took flight, the <color=#3366CC>Hijra</color>, from <color=#3366CC>Mecca</color> to the city of
<color=#3366CC>Medina</color>. Muhammad spent his last ten years in a series of battles to conquer the Arabian region. From 622 to 632,
Muhammad as the leader of a Muslim community in Medina was engaged in a state of war with the Meccans. In the
proceeding decades, the area of <color=#3366CC>Basra</color> was conquered by the Muslims. During the reign of <color=#3366CC>Umar</color>, the Muslim army
found it a suitable place to construct a base. Later the area was settled and a mosque was erected. Madyan was
conquered and settled by Muslims, but the environment was considered harsh and the settlers moved to <color=#3366CC>Kufa</color>. Umar
defeated the rebellion of several Arab tribes in a successful campaign, unifying the entire Arabian peninsula and giving
it stability. Under <color=#3366CC>Uthman</color>'s leadership, the empire, through the <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquest of Persia</color>, expanded into <color=#3366CC>Fars</color> in 650,
some areas of <color=#3366CC>Khorasan</color> in 651, and the conquest of Armenia was begun in the 640s. In this time, the <color=#3366CC>Rashidun</color>
<color=#3366CC>Caliphate</color> extended over the whole Sassanid Persian Empire and to more than two-thirds of the Eastern Roman
Empire. The <color=#3366CC>First Fitna</color>, or the First Islamic Civil War, lasted for the entirety of <color=#3366CC>Ali ibn Abi Talib</color>'s reign. After the
recorded peace treaty with <color=#3366CC>Hassan ibn Ali</color> and the suppression of early <color=#3366CC>Kharijites</color>' disturbances, <color=#3366CC>Muawiyah I</color> acceded to
the position of Caliph.
During this era, Medieval Egypt underwent a profound transformation, moving from a Christian <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> province to
an independent, sovereign Islamic state and a major founding center of the <color=#3366CC>Islamic world</color>. This era permanently
reshaped the region's religion, language, culture, and political governance.
Islamic expansion
The <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquests</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman Empire and Arab wars</color> occurred between 634 and 750. Starting in 633,
Muslims <color=#3366CC>conquered Iraq</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquest of Syria</color> would begin in 634 and would be complete by 638. The <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>
<color=#3366CC>conquest of Egypt</color> started in 639. Before the <color=#3366CC>Muslim invasion of Egypt</color> began, the Eastern Roman Empire had already
lost the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color> and its Arab ally, the <color=#3366CC>Ghassanid Kingdom</color>, to the Muslims. The Muslims would bring Alexandria under
control and the fall of Egypt would be complete by 642. Between 647 and 709, <color=#3366CC>Muslims swept across North Africa</color> and
established their authority over that region.
The site of the Grand Mosque was originally a pagan temple, then a Visigothic Christian church, before the Umayyad
Moors at first converted the building into a mosque and then built a new mosque on the site.
The Transoxiana region was conquered by Qutayba ibn Muslim between 706 and 715 and loosely held by the
Umayyads from 715 to 738. This conquest was consolidated by Nasr ibn Sayyar between 738 and 740. It was under
the Umayyads from 740 to 748 and under the Abbasids after 748. <color=#3366CC>Sindh</color>, attacked in 664, would be subjugated by 712.
Sindh became the easternmost province of the Umayyad. The Umayyad conquest of Hispania (<color=#3366CC>Visigothic Spain</color>) would
begin in 711 and end by 718. The <color=#3366CC>Moors</color>, under Al-Samh ibn Malik, swept up the Iberian peninsula and by 719 overran
Septimania; the area would fall under their full control in 720. With the <color=#3366CC>Islamic conquest of Persia</color>, the Muslim
subjugation of the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> would take place between 711 and 750. The end of the sudden Islamic Caliphate
expansion ended around this time. The final Islamic dominion eroded the areas of the Iron Age Roman Empire in the
Middle East and controlled strategic areas of the Mediterranean.
At the end of the 8th century, the former Western Roman Empire was decentralized and overwhelmingly rural. The
Islamic conquest and rule of Sicily and Malta was a process which started in the 9th century. Islamic rule over Sicily
was effective from 902, and the complete rule of the island lasted from 965 until 1061. The Islamic presence on the
Italian Peninsula was ephemeral and limited mostly to semi-permanent soldier camps.
Caliphs and empire
The <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color>, ruled by the Abbasid dynasty of caliphs, was the third of the Islamic caliphates. Under the
Abbasids, the <color=#3366CC>Islamic Golden Age</color> philosophers, scientists, and engineers of the Islamic world contributed enormously
to technology, both by preserving earlier traditions and by adding their own inventions and innovations. Scientific and
intellectual achievements blossomed in the period.
The Abbasids built their capital in Baghdad after replacing the Umayyad caliphs from all but the Iberian peninsula. The
influence held by Muslim merchants over African-Arabian and Arabian-Asian trade routes was tremendous. As a result,
Islamic civilization grew and expanded on the basis of its merchant economy, in contrast to their Christian, Indian, and
Chinese peers who built societies from an agricultural landholding nobility.
The Abbasids flourished for two centuries but slowly went into decline with the rise to power of the Turkish army they
had created, the <color=#3366CC>Mamluks</color>. Within 150 years of gaining control of Persia, the caliphs were forced to cede power to local
dynastic emirs who only nominally acknowledged their authority. After the Abbasids lost their military dominance, the
Iranian <color=#3366CC>Samanids</color> (or Samanid Empire) rose up in Central Asia.
